questions.question: For $z = 2-3\mathrm{i}$, what is $\operatorname{Im}(z)$?
options: $3\mathrm{i}$
$2-3\mathrm{i}$

questions.question: Which inclusion relation between $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ is correct?
options: Every complex number is real, so the two sets are the same.
Every real number is complex, but some complex numbers are not real.
No real number is complex, because complex means non-real.
$\mathbb{C}\subset\mathbb{R}$, so complex numbers form the smaller set.

questions.question: For $z=a+\mathrm{i}b$, what kind of numbers are $a$ and $b$?
options: Complex numbers with no real part
Real numbers
Only positive integers
Only rational numbers with nonzero denominator

questions.question: When is $a+\mathrm{i}b$ a real number inside $\mathbb{C}$?
options: When $a=0$
When $b=1$
When $a=b$
When $b=0$

questions.question: What condition makes $a+\mathrm{i}b$ purely imaginary?
options: $a=b$

questions.question: Which complex number is not purely imaginary?
options: $0+3\mathrm{i}$
$-4\mathrm{i}$
$2+3\mathrm{i}$
$0-\mathrm{i}$

questions.question: Which description matches the ordered-pair interpretation of $a+\mathrm{i}b$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$?
options: It can be viewed as the unordered set $\{a,b\}$ of two real numbers.
It can be viewed as the ordered pair $(a,b)$ of two real numbers.
It can be viewed as the ordered pair $(b,a)$, imaginary part first.
It is the point of the real line at the real number $a+b$.

questions.question: Which statement about $z=1-\mathrm{i}$ is correct?
options: $z>0$, because its real part $\operatorname{Re}(z)=1$ is positive
$z<0$, because its imaginary part $\operatorname{Im}(z)=-1$ is negative
$z>0$, because its modulus $|z|=\sqrt{2}$ is positive
Neither $z>0$ nor $z<0$ has a meaning in $\mathbb{C}$

questions.question: The real numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy $(x+2y)+\mathrm{i}(x-y)=5+2\mathrm{i}$. What are $x$ and $y$?
options: Not determined: one equation in two unknowns

questions.question: Why is there no order $<$ on $\mathbb{C}$ that obeys all the rules of the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$?
options: Because $\mathbb{C}$ is uncountable, and no uncountable set has a total order
Because pairs $(a,b)$ of real numbers cannot be put in any total order at all
Because such rules make every square at least $0$, while $\mathrm{i}^2=-1$
Because $1$ and $\mathrm{i}$ are different but have the same modulus $1$

questions.question: A complex number $a+\mathrm{i}b$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ is called real when $b=0$ and purely imaginary when $a=0$. Which complex numbers are both real and purely imaginary?
options: None: the real and the purely imaginary numbers are disjoint
Only $0$
Every purely imaginary number, since its square is real
Every real number $a$, since $a=a+0\mathrm{i}$ has imaginary part $0$
